state: implemented and locally validated in draft PR #375; not merged

records.name: Cell lineage, identity and state
records.tldr: A cell’s ancestry, its type and its current activity answer different questions. Similar activity does not prove that two cells share a recent ancestor.
records.summary: Lineage describes descent from earlier cells. A cell type or identity describes a differentiated family, while a state describes context-dependent features such as activation, stress or cycling. A genetic clone has shared ancestry and can be tracked through specified genomic features; an RNA cluster alone does not establish that ancestry. Stem cells can renew and generate descendants; progenitor potential is restricted by the biological context. Differentiation develops specialized properties without requiring every change of state to become a new lineage.

links.label: Lineage tracing on transcriptional landscapes links state to fate during differentiation.

notes: Reference atlases classify measured features. Barcodes or other validated tracing information add ancestry evidence, with their own labeling and sampling limits. Weinreb and colleagues combined expressed barcodes and transcriptomes over time in hematopoiesis; sister-cell analyses exposed fate biases that a single RNA snapshot missed. This does not identify an individual tumor’s origin from its expression profile.

records.name: Epithelium, stroma and tissue compartments
records.tldr: Tissue contains different cell groups and supporting material. Knowing which compartment produced a signal helps explain what the result can mean.
records.summary: Epithelium forms linings, coverings and glands; an epithelial cell is not necessarily malignant. A basement membrane is extracellular supporting material beneath an epithelium, distinct from each cell’s lipid membrane. Stroma includes supporting cells, extracellular matrix and vascular structures, rather than only collagen or fibroblasts. Immune cells and other nonmalignant cells can contribute to a tumor specimen. The relevant compartments depend on the tissue and disease.

links.label: NCI SEER: epithelial organization and basement membrane
A spatially resolved single-cell genomic atlas of the adult human breast.
A single-cell and spatially resolved atlas of human breast cancers.

notes: Bulk RNA or protein measurements combine contributions from sampled cells. A stronger signal can reflect more cells of one type, changed expression within cells, or both. Spatial review and suitable cell markers help test attribution; a mixed-tissue result should not automatically be assigned to cancer cells. Normal and cancer breast atlases provide defined examples of this cellular diversity.

records.name: Organelles and cellular compartments
records.tldr: A cell has compartments with different jobs. A molecule inside one compartment may still be separated from the place where it needs to act.
records.summary: The nucleus houses most cellular DNA; mitochondria have their own genome and participate in energy metabolism and other processes. Ribosomes make polypeptide chains. The endoplasmic reticulum and Golgi process and sort selected membrane or secreted cargo, while lysosomes degrade delivered material in an acidic compartment. That itinerary is not the route of every protein. Cytosol is the fluid outside membrane-bound organelle interiors; cytoplasm includes cytosol and structures outside the nucleus. A vesicle lumen is not cytosol.

links.label: NHGRI: DNA in nuclei and mitochondria
Induction of apoptotic program in cell-free extracts: requirement for dATP and cytochrome c.

notes: Endoplasmic reticulum and estrogen receptor are different meanings of ER; use the full name when context is unclear.
Localization, colocalization, amount, interaction and function need different evidence. More or brighter organelle staining does not by itself measure the rate of material passing through a pathway.

Mitochondria have roles beyond ATP production. Liu and colleagues used cell-free extracts and cytochrome-c depletion/add-back experiments to examine an apoptotic mechanism; this is a defined experimental result, not a universal measurement of cell death.

records.name: Alleles, zygosity and copy state
records.tldr: An allele is a sequence version at a genomic location. Which versions are present and how many DNA copies exist are separate questions.
records.summary: At a diploid location, heterozygous means that the two copies differ in the feature being considered; homozygous means they match. Hemizygous describes a single copy in the specified context. Tumor gains, losses and genome doubling can make a two-copy model inadequate. Loss of heterozygosity means loss of previously different allelic information; it can accompany a deletion or occur while total copy count remains unchanged. Total copy number alone cannot identify which allele was retained.

links.label: Allele-specific genomic data elucidate the role of somatic gain and copy-number neutral loss of heterozygosity in cancer.
Absolute quantification of somatic DNA alterations in human cancer.

notes: Variant allele frequency counts supporting reads or molecules under the assay’s definition. Purity, local copy state, subclonal mixtures and method affect it; it is not directly a cancer-cell percentage or a zygosity call. Phase asks whether specified variants share a DNA copy, a further question that a gene-name match does not answer.

records.name: Epigenetic marks and DNA methylation
records.tldr: Chemical features of DNA and its packaging can influence how genes are used. Their location and cellular context matter; a mark does not have one universal effect.
records.summary: DNA methylation changes a base’s chemical state without substituting the underlying sequence letter. Much human methylation analysis concerns 5-methylcytosine at CpG sites. Histone modifications affect DNA-associated proteins and are distinct from marks on DNA itself. Some regulatory states persist through division; epigenetic does not mean every mark is permanent or transmitted between generations. Promoter methylation can participate in reduced transcription, while patterns elsewhere need their own interpretation.

links.label: Human DNA methylomes at base resolution show widespread epigenomic differences.
A genomic sequencing protocol that yields a positive display of 5-methylcytosine residues in individual DNA strands.

notes: Standard bisulfite analysis changes unmodified cytosine but reads both 5-methylcytosine and 5-hydroxymethylcytosine as C. Oxidative bisulfite methods separate those features through additional chemistry. Ordinary amplified DNA sequence does not preserve this direct chemical measurement.

A methylation signal in mixed tissue is not a percentage of cancer cells with a silenced gene. Cell mixture, genomic location, conversion controls and method resolution matter. Association with low RNA does not establish causation or treatment sensitivity.

records.name: Nonsense-mediated RNA decay
records.tldr: A cell can reduce some RNA messages when translation stops in an unexpected context. A predicted early stop does not guarantee that every message or protein disappears.
records.summary: Nonsense-mediated decay is RNA surveillance coupled to translation termination. Splicing can leave exon junction protein complexes near later joins in the message. Translation can remove junction-associated proteins; early termination while an appropriate complex remains downstream can help recruit decay machinery in one human route. Stop position, exon architecture, proximity to the start and other transcript features affect susceptibility. A common junction-distance shortcut is a hypothesis, not a universal clinical cutoff.

links.label: The exon-exon junction complex provides a binding platform for factors involved in mRNA export and nonsense-mediated mRNA decay.
Translation is required to remove Y14 from mRNAs in the cytoplasm.
Intron function in the nonsense-mediated decay of beta-globin mRNA: indications that pre-mRNA splicing in the nucleus can influence mRNA translation in the cytoplasm.
The rules and impact of nonsense-mediated mRNA decay in human cancers.

notes: Human-cancer analyses found that a model containing several rules described RNA effects better than the junction rule alone; compensation could mask loss at gene level. Test the relevant transcript or allele with controls for RNA quality and cell mixture. Protein identity, persistence and function need separate measurements: RNA decay is distinct from protein degradation.

records.name: V(D)J recombination and receptor assembly
records.tldr: Developing lymphocytes assemble receptor genes from selected DNA segments. Making a receptor is separate from showing what it recognizes or whether it produces a useful response.
records.summary: Variable, diversity and joining segments provide the V, D and J names. Antibody heavy and conventional T-cell-receptor beta chains use VDJ arrangements; antibody light and T-cell-receptor alpha chains use VJ. RAG1/RAG2 recognize recombination signals and initiate DNA cutting; classical non-homologous end-joining repair machinery processes and joins coding ends, adding sequence diversity. Purified-protein cutting experiments and RAG1-deficient mouse experiments established distinct mechanistic requirements. RAG proteins are not the general repair machinery for every DNA break.

links.label: Cleavage at a V(D)J recombination signal requires only RAG1 and RAG2 proteins and occurs in two steps.
RAG-1-deficient mice have no mature B and T lymphocytes.
Immunoglobulin and T Cell Receptor Genes: IMGT(®) and the Birth and Rise of Immunoinformatics.
EuroClonality/BIOMED-2 guidelines for interpretation and reporting of Ig/TCR clonality testing in suspected lymphoproliferations.
Arnal and colleagues: RAG post-cleavage complexes and repair-pathway access

notes: Rearrangement occurs in developing lymphocyte lineages, rather than changing receptor genes in every body cell. Some joins are unproductive; expression and developmental selection are further steps. Later antibody mutation and class switching are different processes.
Receptor sequence or clonality does not establish antigen specificity, tumor recognition or malignant diagnosis. RAG RNA/protein presence alone does not establish active recombination.

records.name: Protein structure, domains and model confidence
records.tldr: A protein’s sequence, folded regions and contacts describe different features. A confident prediction of one region does not establish the whole molecule’s arrangement or function.
records.summary: Primary structure describes sequence; secondary structure describes local arrangements; tertiary structure describes a chain’s organization; quaternary structure describes assembly between chains. These are levels of description, rather than four obligatory stages. A domain is a recognizable structural unit; a motif is a recurring sequence or structural pattern. An interface is a contact surface and can combine residues far apart in sequence. Intrinsically disordered regions can have normal functions without one stable isolated fold.
notes: Experimental structures reflect particular preparations and conditions, and may omit flexible regions. In AlphaFold2, pLDDT concerns local structural confidence, while predicted aligned error helps assess uncertainty in relative region placement. A confident domain cannot certify a proposed inter-domain pocket or contact. Neither score measures binding affinity, protein abundance, a variant’s functional effect or clinical benefit.

records.name: Binding affinity, occupancy and enzyme kinetics
records.tldr: Binding strength, the fraction of sites occupied and the speed of a reaction describe different things. Each measurement needs its experimental conditions.
records.summary: For a simple reversible binding equilibrium, Kd is the product of free partner concentrations divided by complex concentration; lower Kd means tighter binding under those conditions. For identical independent sites with one ligand and no competition, fractional occupancy is L / (Kd + L), where L is free ligand concentration. Half occupancy occurs at L = Kd in that model. Total added ligand need not equal free ligand. Affinity for one partner does not establish specificity against other partners.

links.label: A guide to simple, direct, and quantitative in vitro binding assays.
Classroom model and derivation of Michaelis-Menten parameters; not an enzyme experiment

notes: For a suitable Michaelis-Menten enzyme model, Km is the substrate concentration at half the maximum initial reaction rate. It depends on the catalytic mechanism and conditions and is not generally Kd. Turnover concerns reaction cycling, not binding strength.

IC50 is half inhibition of a specified assay response; EC50 describes half of a defined functional response change. Substrate/ATP concentrations, enzyme or receptor amount, timing and assay design affect these measures. A biochemical inhibition value, a cell-growth value and a clinical outcome are separate evidence.

records.name: Feedback, feedforward and signaling dynamics
records.tldr: A signal can change the circuit that produced it. Returning inhibition, returning reinforcement and a separate forward route can create different responses over time.
records.summary: Negative feedback returns a restraining effect to an upstream process; positive feedback reinforces it. These names describe direction, not clinical desirability. Feedforward sends an input through direct and indirect routes to an output without a returning connection. Connections, delays and cell state can produce transient, sustained or oscillating behavior. A positive loop does not always make an irreversible switch, and rebound need not require a new mutation.

links.label: Growth factor-induced MAPK network topology shapes Erk response determining PC-12 cell fate.
mTOR inhibition induces upstream receptor tyrosine kinase signaling and activates Akt.
Structure and function of the feed-forward loop network motif.

notes: Santos and colleagues altered feedback arrangements in a PC12 differentiation model, demonstrating that input context can change network dynamics and cell response. O’Reilly and colleagues examined released feedback after mTOR inhibition in cancer models with patient-tumor pharmacodynamic observations. Neither study establishes universal tumor wiring or combination-treatment benefit.

Use time-resolved measurements and controlled perturbation of the proposed connection, with exposure and viability controls. Similar curves can arise from different circuits; a diagram or one late signal cannot identify the mechanism.

records.name: Receptor reserve and system-dependent response
records.tldr: A cell can sometimes reach its largest measured response without occupying every receptor. Receptor amount and downstream amplification help determine that response.
records.summary: Receptor reserve describes a system in which maximal functional response can be obtained before all available receptors are occupied. Occupancy and response can therefore have different concentration-response curves. Operational receptor models separate binding, receptor abundance or activation, and downstream transduction. An EC50 lower than a binding Kd is not on its own evidence of tighter binding. Changing receptor expression or amplification can alter apparent potency and the observed maximum of a partial agonist.

links.label: A Receptor Model With Binding Affinity, Activation Efficacy, and Signal Amplification Parameters for Complex Fractional Response Versus Occupancy Data.

notes: Black and Leff developed an operational model; the later two-state model explicitly separates binding, activation and amplification and examines receptor-reserve data. These are quantitative pharmacology frameworks, not clinical dose-selection rules. Testing reserve requires functional and binding evidence or controlled changes in receptor availability with appropriate model checks.

records.name: Biased agonism and pathway-dependent receptor response
records.tldr: Two ligands at the same receptor can favor measured response pathways differently. That comparison depends on the reference ligand, assays and cellular system.
records.summary: Biased agonism compares the relative signaling behavior of ligands across specified outputs at the same receptor. Binding, intrinsic receptor activation, pathway amplification and baseline activity can contribute differently to observed curves. A potency difference between two assays does not by itself isolate ligand-specific bias. Preserve the reference ligand, endpoints, receptor expression, timing and model assumptions used to estimate it.

links.label: Estimation of ligand affinity constants for receptor states in functional studies involving the allosteric modulation of G protein-coupled receptors: implications for ligand bias.
Estimation of the receptor-state affinity constants of ligands in functional studies using wild type and constitutively active mutant receptors: Implications for estimation of agonist bias.
A Receptor Model With Binding Affinity, Activation Efficacy, and Signal Amplification Parameters for Complex Fractional Response Versus Occupancy Data.

notes: Ehlert and colleagues’ methods analyzed receptor-state affinities and pathway sensitivity using analytical proofs, simulations and previously published data. The constitutively active-mutant approach assumes that the mutation changes receptor-state equilibrium without changing ligand affinities and requires checking that assumption. These method studies do not establish clinical superiority of a biased ligand or validate every cellular assay.

records.name: Promoters, enhancers and transcription factors
records.tldr: Genes are regulated through DNA regions, binding proteins and cellular context. A bound regulator or accessible DNA region does not prove that a gene’s output changed.
records.summary: A promoter is a DNA region where transcription machinery assembles. Enhancers influence transcription through regulatory interactions, sometimes across a long linear distance brought together in three-dimensional space. Transcription factors recognize sequence features and participate in regulatory networks. Chromatin state and cellular partners affect access and function. Regulation also occurs through RNA processing and removal, translation, and protein modification or turnover.

links.label: Lambert and colleagues: The Human Transcription Factors (review and catalog)

notes: RNA measurements, chromatin accessibility, protein occupancy and reporter activity answer different questions. Binding or an open region alone does not establish regulation of a particular gene. Controlled perturbation can test a proposed causal connection, with controls for indirect effects and assay context.

records.name: Central dogma and molecular information flow
records.tldr: DNA copying, making RNA and making a protein are different processes. Following the route helps identify what each molecular test actually measured.
records.summary: Replication makes DNA from DNA. Transcription uses a DNA template to make RNA. Translation reads the coding sequence of a message in three-base codons to build a polypeptide; the transcript and reading frame matter. Functional noncoding RNAs do not need to become protein. Reverse transcription copies RNA into DNA in relevant viral and retrotransposon contexts. This information-flow map is not a guarantee that every DNA change produces a measured RNA or protein change.

links.label: NHGRI: RNA, coding/noncoding functions and reverse transcription

notes: RNA processing, translation, folding, modification, localization and turnover can alter the path from a coding sequence to a functional product. DNA presence, RNA abundance, intact protein, location and activity require their own evidence. Neither a gene-level RNA count nor a sequence prediction establishes a fixed protein amount or clinical effect.

records.name: Cell membrane
records.tldr: The cell membrane forms a selective boundary. Binding at the surface, entering a vesicle and reaching the cell’s internal working fluid are different steps.
records.summary: A lipid bilayer and its proteins separate the cell from its surroundings. Permeability depends on size, charge and chemical properties, rather than a universal small-molecule versus antibody rule. Passive movement follows the relevant gradient; active transport uses energy directly or through a coupled gradient. Endocytosis encloses material in a membrane-bound compartment. Delivery to cytosol or another target compartment requires further steps. Cytosol is fluid outside organelle interiors; cytoplasm includes that fluid and structures outside the nucleus.
notes: Surface-associated fluorescence does not establish internalization or cytosolic delivery. A membrane-exclusion dye tests the integrity property resolved by that assay; it does not certify every cell function.

records.name: Cell cycle
records.tldr: Cells preparing to divide pass through regulated stages for growth, DNA copying and chromosome separation. Some cells remain functional while outside that cycle.
records.summary: G1 prepares the cell, S copies DNA, and G2 precedes the mitotic phase. Mitosis separates nuclear chromosomes; cytokinesis separates cytoplasm into daughter cells. G0 describes a noncycling state, which need not mean death or loss of function. Cyclins, CDKs and checkpoints regulate transitions, and their alteration can contribute to cancer without making every checkpoint absent or guaranteeing error-free division. Cell-cycle checkpoints and immune checkpoints describe different biological processes.

links.label: Assaying Cell Cycle Status Using Flow Cytometry.
Doublet discrimination in DNA cell-cycle analysis.

notes: DNA-content measurements commonly group G0/G1 and G2/M because each pair shares a DNA-content range. Appropriate additional markers and doublet discrimination are needed: two cells can resemble one cell with more DNA.

A Ki-67-positive fraction or snapshot phase distribution is not a division rate or a population doubling time. Time-resolved proliferation and cell-loss measurements answer further questions. CDK4/6 inhibitors and spindle-directed drugs affect different parts of the cycle.

records.name: Cell division
records.tldr: Cell division produces daughter cells for growth and renewal. Chemotherapy can disrupt this process and can also affect cells through mechanisms beyond division.
records.summary: DNA copying, chromosome segregation and cytokinesis are distinct steps; errors or unequal allocation can make daughters differ. Many cytotoxic drugs affect DNA or microtubules, with drug-specific dependence on cell-cycle state. Normal renewing tissues can also be affected. Division history cannot be read directly from a mutation count: damage, repair, selection and other processes contribute. Ki-67 staining and a mitotic count describe particular sampled properties, not a universal rate of cell production.

links.label: NCI: chemotherapy mechanisms and healthy-cell effects
Neurotoxic mechanisms of paclitaxel are local to the distal axon and independent of transport defects.
Assaying Cell Cycle Status Using Flow Cytometry.

notes: Growth arrest and cell death need separate measurements. A population count reflects both production and loss. In adult mouse sensory-neuron cultures, paclitaxel disrupted distal axon growth without requiring cell division; this defined experimental model does not predict every clinical toxicity or treatment effect.

Side effects are not a test of whether chemotherapy is controlling a tumor. NCI explicitly separates those observations; clinical assessment needs the appropriate examination, imaging or other response evaluation. A proliferation-marker fraction also does not by itself measure treatment benefit.

records.name: Differentiation
records.tldr: Differentiation develops specialized cellular properties. In pathology, resemblance to a mature tissue can contribute to grading, whose meaning depends on the cancer.
records.summary: Differentiation concerns development of specialized cell features and functions. Stem or progenitor ancestry, current state and genetic clone are distinct questions. In cancer pathology, well or poorly differentiated describes resemblance to a mature tissue within the applicable classification; it is not a universal rule that one category grows at a particular speed. Tumor plasticity can change marker expression or lineage programs. A present-day expression cluster alone does not reconstruct the cell’s ancestry or prove a reversal of its developmental history.

links.label: Lineage tracing on transcriptional landscapes links state to fate during differentiation.

records.name: Epithelial-mesenchymal transition & drug efflux
records.tldr: Epithelial cells can change a coordinated set of properties, sometimes entering intermediate states. The consequences depend on the cells and the experimental or clinical context.
records.summary: Epithelial-mesenchymal transition describes coordinated changes in cellular organization and programs, occurring in development, repair and disease. It is not a binary switch defined by one marker. Primary skin and mammary tumor studies identified intermediate epithelial/mesenchymal states with differing properties. Associations with migration, stem-like features, immune effects or drug resistance require context-specific evidence; they should not all be assigned automatically to every mesenchymal signal.

links.label: Guidelines and definitions for research on epithelial-mesenchymal transition.
Identification of the tumour transition states occurring during EMT.
Epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition is not required for lung metastasis but contributes to chemoresistance.

notes: Use multiple cellular properties, suitable spatial attribution and, when testing a transition, time or lineage evidence. Bulk mesenchymal RNA can reflect nonmalignant stromal cells. Mouse lineage-tracing experiments that examined metastasis and chemotherapy resistance support conclusions within their reporter/model settings; an EMT label alone does not establish sensitivity or select treatment.
records.analogy: A brick in a wall (epithelial cell) turning into a nomad: it lets go of its neighbours, packs pumps to spit out poison, and puts on camouflage. The wall-brick was easy to hit; the nomad is not.
interventions: Payloads with low efflux susceptibility (sac-TMT's belotecan derivative claims this) and radiation (efflux-independent)
TGF-β pathway blockade (mostly failed so far)
Immune approaches to overcome exclusion (STING, radiation)

records.name: Germline vs somatic mutations
records.tldr: A DNA change can be inherited, newly constitutional or acquired in a cell lineage. A change found in a tumor is not automatically tumor-specific.
records.summary: Inherited germline variants came through an egg or sperm and are generally present across many tissues. A de novo constitutional variant need not have been inherited from a parent. Changes arising after fertilization can create mosaic distributions. Somatic variants occur in body-cell lineages, including normal tissues as well as cancers. Origin, distribution, harmfulness and transmissibility are separate questions; neither a variant class nor a large read fraction settles them.

links.label: MedlinePlus Genetics: inherited, de novo and mosaic variants
Personalized genomic analyses for cancer mutation discovery and interpretation.
High-intensity sequencing reveals the sources of plasma circulating cell-free DNA variants.
NCI: inherited-cancer testing, tumor testing and bounded negative results

notes: Suitable tumor/normal comparison can help attribute origin, but blood can carry acquired hematopoietic clones. Plasma variants can arise from those clones as well as a tumor. Mosaicism, contamination, specimen suitability and assay limits require assessment rather than automatic subtraction of every blood-matching variant.

Tumor sequencing is distinct from a clinical hereditary test. A negative result is bounded by its specimen, covered genes, detectable change classes and method; research matched-normal analysis does not automatically supply a hereditary-risk report.

records.name: DNA
records.tldr: DNA stores sequence information. Its packaging, copying and use as a template for RNA are different processes.
records.summary: DNA contains nucleotide chains with a sugar–phosphate backbone and the bases A, T, C and G. Complementary A–T and C–G pairing joins antiparallel strands. Nuclear chromosomes contain DNA associated with proteins as chromatin; nucleosomes organize DNA around histones. Mitochondria carry a separate genome. A gene is a functional region within DNA, rather than an entire chromosome. Replication copies DNA, while transcription produces RNA from a selected template. Packaging and gene presence do not establish active transcription or a functional protein.

records.name: RNA
records.tldr: RNA is a family of molecules with several jobs. Messenger RNA provides a protein-making template; other RNAs help build, regulate or carry out cellular processes.
records.summary: RNA uses ribose and usually uracil in place of DNA’s thymine. It is often single-stranded but can fold through internal pairing. Messenger RNA carries a coding template; ribosomal RNA contributes to ribosome structure and catalysis; transfer RNA brings amino acids; regulatory RNAs influence other molecules. Many nuclear messages receive a 5-prime cap and poly(A) tail and have introns removed by splicing before translation, but these features are not universal to all RNAs. Ribosomes read a coding sequence in codons to produce a polypeptide; processing, folding and localization follow.

links.label: NHGRI: RNA roles, processing and reverse transcription

notes: RNA abundance reflects production, processing and degradation. Short sequencing reads do not prove that a full-length intact message was captured. A noncoding RNA can function without becoming a protein, and reverse transcription copies RNA into DNA in relevant biological contexts. RNA amount does not determine a fixed protein amount or activity.

After successful delivery, a supplied ordinary mRNA can be translated at cytoplasmic ribosomes; that translation step does not require the message to enter the nucleus. Supplying a message, measuring endogenous tumor RNA and demonstrating nuclear DNA modification are separate observations. The NHGRI vaccine example illustrates supplied RNA instructions, not a general cancer-efficacy claim.

records.name: Gene
records.tldr: A gene is a DNA region that produces a functional RNA message. Some messages encode proteins; others work as RNA.
records.summary: A protein-coding gene supplies RNA that can be translated into a polypeptide, while a noncoding RNA gene produces a functional RNA. Promoters and other regulatory regions influence transcription in a cell-dependent context. One gene can have several transcript versions. Exons are retained regions of a specified processed transcript and can include untranslated sequence; introns are removed by splicing. Coding sequence is the translated part of a coding message. A gene name alone does not specify a transcript, coding interval or protein product.
notes: Preserve the reference sequence, accession and version when describing a variant consequence. DNA sequencing, gene-level RNA counts and protein assays measure different objects; a pooled count does not establish every isoform or an intact active protein. Gene and protein names are often shared, so identify which molecule an assay or drug claim concerns.

records.name: Protein
records.tldr: Proteins are amino-acid products that provide structure, catalysis, transport and signaling. A detected fragment and a complete working protein are different findings.
records.summary: Amino acids join through peptide bonds into polypeptide chains; linked amino acids are residues. Peptide and protein usage overlaps without a universal length boundary. A protein may contain one or several chains, folded domains and flexible regions. Processing, chemical modifications, localization, production and degradation affect its form and behavior. Genes specify coding templates, but a DNA or RNA finding does not measure the resulting protein’s intact structure or activity.
notes: An antibody may recognize an epitope on more than one product form or a remaining fragment. Many mass-spectrometry workflows digest proteins into peptides: a shared detected peptide cannot distinguish every full-length form. A candidate peptide sequence also does not establish its display by HLA. Separate assays address amount, location, intact form, function and antigen presentation.

records.name: Enzyme
records.tldr: An enzyme speeds a chemical reaction and is reused through its reaction cycle. Binding to an enzyme does not by itself show that the reaction or a cell response changed.
records.summary: Catalysis lowers a reaction’s activation barrier without supplying an unlimited energy source. Most familiar enzymes are proteins, while some RNAs also catalyze reactions. Active-site interactions help chemistry; other binding sites can regulate activity. Binding, catalytic rate, substrate preference and activity in a cell are different properties. An inhibitor can act through the active site or another mechanism, and turnover rates are not one universal number.

links.label: A guide to simple, direct, and quantitative in vitro binding assays.

notes: Affinity, specificity, Kd, Km and assay IC50 answer distinct questions. Report the model, free concentrations, substrates, cofactors and timing. Kinases, PARP and topoisomerases illustrate oncology enzyme targets, but binding alone does not establish useful cellular inhibition or patient benefit.

records.name: Gene expression
records.tldr: Gene expression produces RNA and, for coding messages, protein. Measurements at those steps are related but do not answer the same question.
records.summary: Transcription makes RNA from DNA; translation reads a coding message in codons to make a polypeptide. This information-flow description does not require every RNA to become protein. A promoter recruits transcription machinery. Enhancers influence transcription through regulatory interactions that can span distant DNA positions. Transcription factors recognize sequence features and participate in regulation. Chromatin, RNA processing and turnover, translation, protein processing and degradation all influence the eventual product. A transcript’s frame and reference context matter when interpreting a sequence change.

links.label: Gene expression analysis identifies global gene dosage sensitivity in cancer.

notes: DNA presence, regulator binding, accessible chromatin and increased RNA are separate observations. RNA sequencing samples messages; chromatin-accessibility and protein-binding assays address different properties. Reporter or controlled perturbation experiments test particular regulatory hypotheses, with controls for indirect effects.

RNA abundance does not provide a fixed conversion to protein abundance or activity. Gene dosage can contribute to RNA variation, but a population association or statistical correction does not establish a particular protein amount, growth dependence or therapeutic response in one sample.

records.name: RNA splicing
records.tldr: RNA processing removes introns and joins retained exons. Different processing choices can produce different messages without changing the underlying gene sequence.
records.summary:
Splicing processes an initial RNA transcript. Exons are retained in a specified product and may contain untranslated sequence; introns are removed. For many nuclear pre-mRNAs, a spliceosome made of RNA and proteins recognizes boundary and regulatory sequences. The donor site starts an intron and the acceptor site ends it. Alternative choices yield transcript isoforms; a variant can alter exon inclusion, intron retention or use of a cryptic site. Exon skipping is not automatically a frameshift: the coding sequence and resulting joins matter. An altered message may undergo nonsense-mediated decay or produce a changed protein, but neither outcome follows from a prediction alone.

Cancer-associated splicing changes can arise through altered RNA-processing factors or their expression. SF3B1, SRSF2, U2AF1 and ZRSR2 illustrate studied factors; AR-V7 and BCL2L1 illustrate named transcript contexts. The linked review describes disease-specific mechanisms and therapeutic research. An altered transcript alone does not establish an intact abnormal protein, immune presentation, a therapeutic dependency or patient benefit. Free-drug development and a conjugated payload also require their own construct-specific evidence.

links.label: Bradley & Anczuków, RNA splicing dysregulation and the hallmarks of cancer (Nature Reviews Cancer 2023)
Intron function in the nonsense-mediated decay of beta-globin mRNA: indications that pre-mRNA splicing in the nucleus can influence mRNA translation in the cytoplasm.

notes: Leading programmes: Abdel-Wahab (MSK) on spliceosome mutations; Bradley (Fred Hutch) on splicing and neoantigens; Ebert (Dana-Farber) on SF3B1 in MDS.

A junction read supports a local RNA join, not necessarily a complete isoform. Gene-level counts can hide transcript differences. RNA quality, read coverage, reference version and cell mixture affect interpretation; protein quantity and function need separate evidence.

The pathway drawing groups possible consequences studied in particular cancer systems. Its arrows do not mean that every splice change causes every listed outcome; protein formation, presentation and functional dependence require their own evidence.
records.analogy: Splicing is like editing a recording into different versions. A changed edit can alter the final product, but the RNA join alone does not show which complete protein is made or what it does.
interventions: Spliceosome modulators (H3B-8800 negative; next generation in development)
PRMT5 inhibitors in MTAP-deleted and splicing-mutant cancers
Antisense oligonucleotides to redirect splicing (AR-V7, BCL2L1)

records.name: Mutation
records.tldr: A DNA variant describes a sequence change relative to a reference. Its origin, effect and clinical importance require separate evidence.
records.summary: A single-nucleotide substitution changes one base. Insertions and deletions change sequence length; copy-number and structural alterations affect larger regions and can overlap in category. In a specified coding transcript, missense changes alter an amino acid, synonymous changes preserve it, and nonsense changes introduce a stop. A net coding indel not divisible by three can shift the reading frame; an indel outside coding sequence is not automatically a frameshift. Transcript and reference versions determine the description.

links.label: HGVS: measured and predicted sequence consequences

notes: A DNA rearrangement, a joined RNA and a protein fusion are different observations. A predicted splice or protein consequence remains a prediction until supported at the relevant molecular level. Synonymous does not mean incapable of affecting RNA processing. Preserve genome build, accession/version, tested regions, detectable change classes and limits; pathogenicity or drug sensitivity does not follow from variant class alone.

records.name: Ligand
records.tldr: A ligand binds a molecular partner. Binding does not necessarily activate a receptor or prove that a treatment will help.
records.summary: Hormones, growth factors and other molecules can bind receptors, but ligand describes the interaction rather than one functional effect. A bound ligand may activate a specified response, oppose another ligand, or show no effect in that assay. Some targeting ligands localize a payload. An accessible binding address need not be a cancer’s growth driver; delivery, intracellular action and clinical benefit require further evidence.

links.label: An allosteric mechanism for activation of the kinase domain of epidermal growth factor receptor.
Engagement of the PD-1 immunoinhibitory receptor by a novel B7 family member leads to negative regulation of lymphocyte activation.
Fibroblast activation protein, a dual specificity serine protease expressed in reactive human tumor stromal fibroblasts.
Functional domains of the human estrogen receptor.
Mapping and characterization of the functional domains responsible for the differential activity of the A and B isoforms of the human progesterone receptor.

notes: An extracellular EGF ligand can change intracellular kinase signaling without entering the cell. Estrogen and progesterone bind their distinct intracellular receptors, which can regulate transcription with different forms and cellular partners. PD-1 engagement can restrain responding T-cell activity, so receptor activation is not always activation of tumor growth. FAP is a surface protease used as a targeting address, not a hormone/growth-factor receptor in this comparison.

Keep free versus added ligand, binding conditions, receptor accessibility, receiving cell, endpoint and time with the result. Surface staining, purified binding and living-cell response are separate assays. Growth dependence requires an appropriate functional perturbation; none of these observations alone establishes clinical eligibility.

records.name: Receptor
records.tldr: Receptors connect molecular recognition to a cellular response through several mechanisms. Their presence and their activity are separate findings.
records.summary: Receptors can be on the surface or inside a cell. Ligand-gated ion channels regulate ion passage; G-protein-coupled receptors act through G proteins; enzyme-linked receptors can contain an enzyme or recruit a separate one. Intracellular nuclear receptors can regulate transcription with cellular partners. A surface signal can ultimately alter genes, while nuclear-receptor family membership does not fix every molecule permanently in the nucleus or require every effect to use new transcription.

links.label: Cell membrane and nuclear estrogen receptors (ERs) originate from a single transcript: studies of ERalpha and ERbeta expressed in Chinese hamster ovary cells.

notes: Defined engineered estrogen-receptor experiments detected nuclear and membrane pools; they do not establish a universal proportion in human tumors. Distinguish receptor identity, location, accessible binding and measured function. A positive stain or fluorescence intensity is not automatically a calibrated receptor count, pathway dependence or drug sensitivity.

records.name: Agonist and antagonist
records.tldr: Agonists promote a specified receptor response; antagonists oppose agonist action. The labels depend on the measured system, and strong binding does not necessarily mean strong activation.
records.summary: A full agonist can reach a system’s maximal measured response. A partial agonist has lower activating capacity; its observed maximum depends on receptor amount and amplification and is not defined by giving a smaller dose of a full agonist. Competing partial agonists can reduce a full agonist’s response when they replace it. A neutral antagonist opposes agonist action without changing agonist-independent baseline activity; an inverse agonist reduces that activity when it is measurable. Antagonism need not use the agonist’s binding site.

links.label: Inverse agonist activity of beta-adrenergic antagonists.
International Union of Pharmacology Committee on Receptor Nomenclature and Drug Classification. XXXVIII. Update on terms and symbols in quantitative pharmacology.

notes: Kd describes binding under specified conditions. Functional EC50 describes half of the compound’s defined response change in that assay. Measure concentration curves, baseline, a reference agonist, receptor/system context, timing and toxicity controls. Suppressing a signal through toxicity does not prove inverse agonism. Receptor efficacy is not clinical efficacy.

Chidiac and colleagues examined agonist-independent beta-adrenergic signaling in expressed-receptor systems. This establishes a mechanistic distinction in those systems, rather than classifying every ligand in every tissue.

records.name: Signalling pathway
records.tldr: A signaling pathway connects an input to cellular changes. Real pathways branch, interact and feed back, so one changed marker does not describe the whole network.
records.summary: Signal transduction uses receptors, second messengers, switches, scaffolds, enzymes and gene regulation in intersecting networks. Not every component is a kinase: RAS is a switch regulated by GTP binding and hydrolysis, and scaffolds organize partners. Kinases can modify proteins or lipids. Responses may involve movement, metabolism, growth, survival or differentiation. The RAS–RAF–MEK–ERK and PI3K–AKT–mTOR systems are examples, rather than a single universal surface-to-nucleus chain.

links.label: Growth factor-induced MAPK network topology shapes Erk response determining PC-12 cell fate.
An allosteric mechanism for activation of the kinase domain of epidermal growth factor receptor.

notes: Time, input, cell type and feedback affect interpretation. An isolated-enzyme assay, one cellular phosphosite and a growth/death outcome measure different properties. Test dependence with suitable functional outcomes and an independent perturbation, controlling exposure, cell entry and unrelated effects.

records.name: Kinase
records.tldr: A kinase transfers a phosphate group to a substrate. The effect depends on which molecule and site are modified.
records.summary: Many protein kinases transfer phosphate from ATP to selected substrate residues, commonly serine, threonine or tyrosine, leaving ADP. Phosphatases remove phosphate through a different reaction, rather than simply making ATP by reversing kinase activity. Kinases can also modify lipids, as PI3K does. Protein amount is distinct from catalytic activity, and not every relay protein is a kinase. In the defined EGFR asymmetric-dimer mechanism, activation-loop phosphorylation was not required for activation.

links.label: An allosteric mechanism for activation of the kinase domain of epidermal growth factor receptor.

notes: Assay ATP/substrate concentrations, enzyme amount, timing and endpoint matter. A lower cellular phosphosite signal is not automatically direct inhibition, suppression of an entire pathway or reduced growth. Active-site, allosteric and other inhibitory mechanisms need their own evidence.

records.name: Phosphorylation
records.tldr: Adding phosphate can change a protein’s behavior in several ways. The site and cellular context determine whether a measured change indicates activation, inhibition or something else.
records.summary: Protein kinases commonly transfer phosphate from ATP to a substrate, producing ADP. Protein phosphatases remove phosphate by hydrolysis without regenerating ATP. A modification can affect catalysis, binding, localization or interactions; sites on one protein can have different functions. Src experiments demonstrated an inhibitory tail-phosphorylation mechanism in their defined preparation, so phosphorylation should not be treated as universal activation.

links.label: Dephosphorylation or antibody binding to the carboxy terminus stimulates pp60c-src.
Ischemia in tumors induces early and sustained phosphorylation changes in stress kinase pathways but does not affect global protein levels.

notes: A phosphosite signal depends on modified molecules, parent-protein amount, recovery and measurement. It is not automatically site occupancy, the fraction modified at that site. A parent-normalized ratio may be informative without becoming an absolute occupancy percentage. Retain site identity/localization confidence, method, specimen handling and time.

This modifies existing molecules and is distinct from changing DNA sequence, RNA production or mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation. One site alone need not identify the responsible enzyme or the state of a whole pathway.

records.name: Pathway activation state (phosphosignalling)
records.tldr: Pathway activity is a question about a specified biological response. Protein amount, individual phosphorylation sites and downstream RNA patterns provide different evidence.
records.summary: Phosphoproteomics and other protein assays can examine specified signaling modifications, with site-specific and context-specific meaning. A site can activate, inhibit, recruit a partner or have an unresolved role. Relative phosphosite intensity also depends on parent-protein amount and sample handling; it is not automatically absolute occupancy. Transcript signatures provide another, often indirect, view. Define the proposed pathway output, timing and cell population instead of equating one marker with the whole circuit.

links.label: Dephosphorylation or antibody binding to the carboxy terminus stimulates pp60c-src.
Ischemia in tumors induces early and sustained phosphorylation changes in stress kinase pathways but does not affect global protein levels.
Growth factor-induced MAPK network topology shapes Erk response determining PC-12 cell fate.

notes: Pair pathway readouts with appropriate controlled perturbations and functional measurements when testing dependence. A changed phosphosite or expression signature does not by itself establish growth inhibition, drug sensitivity or clinical benefit.

records.name: Variant allele frequency (VAF)
records.tldr: Variant allele frequency is the fraction of informative reads or molecules that support a variant under a test’s definition. It is not directly the fraction of cancer cells.
records.summary: Read-based VAF divides variant-supporting reads by informative reads at the locus. Some assays instead report a molecule-based measure, so keep the laboratory’s definition. Tumor purity, local allele-specific copy number, ploidy, subclonal mixture and assay behavior affect the value. VAF alone cannot assign zygosity, variant origin, the number of clones or a cancer-cell percentage. Changes over time in plasma also require attention to specimen and non-tumor DNA contributors.

links.label: Li et al., Standards and guidelines for the interpretation and reporting of sequence variants in cancer: AMP, ASCO and CAP joint consensus (Journal of Molecular Diagnostics 2017)
Absolute quantification of somatic DNA alterations in human cancer.
Allele-specific genomic data elucidate the role of somatic gain and copy-number neutral loss of heterozygosity in cancer.
High-intensity sequencing reveals the sources of plasma circulating cell-free DNA variants.

records.name: Genome-wide loss of heterozygosity (gLOH)
records.tldr: This assay-defined score summarizes genomic regions that lost previously different allelic information. It can reflect a past repair defect, including changes that preserve total DNA copy count.
records.summary:
Loss of heterozygosity means loss of previously distinct allelic information at a locus. It can accompany copy loss or occur with a copy-neutral allelic change; tumor purity and ploidy complicate inference. Genome-wide loss of heterozygosity summarizes affected interrogated regions according to the assay’s definition. It is studied as a genomic scar associated with some homologous-recombination-repair defects, rather than a direct measurement of present repair function.

The threshold belongs to the assay and setting. ARIEL2 part 1 prespecified 14 percent or more as LOH high in its ovarian-cancer analysis; this does not establish a universal cutoff. Pan-cancer studies found elevated gLOH associated with biallelic BRCA1/2 alterations and with a core set of other repair-gene alterations, with effects differing by cancer context. Monoallelic calls and an HRR-gene-list label are not interchangeable with those findings. TP53 loss was independently associated with gLOH in the Westphalen analysis.

In 3,476 prostate tumors, Chung and colleagues found BRCA1/2, ATR and FANCA alterations associated with high gLOH, while CDK12-altered tumors, about 6 percent of that cohort, were infrequently gLOH high. The study did not correlate these findings with clinical outcomes. Such associations support gene-specific biological questions; they do not establish an individual patient’s drug benefit or current treatment eligibility.

links.label: Chung et al., JCO Precision Oncology 2019: prospective comprehensive genomic profiling of 3,476 primary and metastatic prostate tumours
Sokol et al., JCO Precision Oncology 2020: pan-cancer analysis of BRCA1 and BRCA2 genomic alterations and their association with genomic instability as measured by genome-wide loss of heterozygosity
Westphalen et al., Clinical Cancer Research 2022: pan-cancer analysis of homologous recombination repair-associated gene alterations and genome-wide loss-of-heterozygosity score
Swisher et al., Lancet Oncology 2017 (ARIEL2 part 1): rucaparib in relapsed, platinum-sensitive high-grade ovarian carcinoma
Abida et al., Journal of Clinical Oncology 2020 (TRITON2): rucaparib in men with metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer harbouring a BRCA1 or BRCA2 alteration
Allele-specific genomic data elucidate the role of somatic gain and copy-number neutral loss of heterozygosity in cancer.
Absolute quantification of somatic DNA alterations in human cancer.

notes: A scar is different from a present functional defect. gLOH does not by itself establish which repair gene is affected, whether both alleles are inactivated, or whether repair remains impaired. A tumor can retain an earlier genomic scar after its functional state changes.

There is no single gLOH-high cutoff across assays and cancers. ARIEL2 part 1 used a prespecified assay threshold in ovarian carcinoma. Preserve the assay, specimen and reporting context, including uncertainty near a categorical threshold.

Tumor sequencing and clinical hereditary testing answer different questions. The historical TRITON2 study reported similar objective response rates in germline- and somatic-BRCA groups in its enrolled prostate-cancer population; that result is not a current treatment-access rule or evidence that a negative hereditary assay excludes acquired tumor variants.

records.name: Gene amplification and copy-number change
records.tldr: Cancer cells often have extra copies of a growth gene (amplification) or have lost copies of a protective one (deletion), rather than a spelling change within the gene. Extra copies of HER2 or MYCN are classic examples that change treatment.
records.summary: Amplification (detected by FISH, ISH or NGS copy-number calls) drives overexpression: HER2 in breast and gastric cancer, MYCN in high-risk neuroblastoma, MET amplification as a resistance route to EGFR inhibitors, CCNE1 in ovarian and gastric cancer, MDM2 in liposarcoma, CDK4 in glioma. Deletions remove tumour suppressors: del(17p)/TP53 in CLL and myeloma (predicting chemo-resistance), CDKN2A/B in glioma (defining grade 4), MTAP (creating a PRMT5 vulnerability), 9p21 loss linked to immunotherapy resistance. Loss of heterozygosity and large-scale copy changes are summed into genomic-scar scores used to infer HRD and predict PARP inhibitor benefit.

links.label: Absolute quantification of somatic DNA alterations in human cancer.
Gene expression analysis identifies global gene dosage sensitivity in cancer.

notes: Total copy count, allele identity, RNA abundance and protein activity are separate measurements. Purity, ploidy and the assay’s definition affect copy calls. Fehrmann and colleagues related copy number to expression after modeling shared transcriptional components in large datasets; that association does not promise a fixed protein increase, target dependence or treatment benefit in a particular tumor.

records.name: Immunoglobulin and T-cell receptor clonality testing
records.tldr: Receptor-gene patterns can provide evidence of a clonal lymphocyte population. The result must be interpreted with the tissue findings and does not diagnose cancer by itself.
records.summary:
Developing lymphocytes rearrange antigen-receptor genes. Shared rearrangements can support common ancestry, but a detected clonal pattern is not synonymous with malignancy, and a negative assay does not exclude it. Sampling, reactive expansions, multiple alleles, primer coverage and technical artifacts affect interpretation. The number of peaks is not a direct count of clones.

The European BIOMED-2 collaboration standardised the assay into 107 primers in 18 multiplex tubes covering the immunoglobulin heavy chain in two configurations, the kappa and lambda light chains, the T-cell receptor beta, gamma and delta loci, and the BCL1-IGH and BCL2-IGH translocations, read by heteroduplex analysis or fragment sizing. The EuroClonality-NGS successor sequences the amplicons instead of sizing them, which both improves resolution and produces a patient-specific sequence that can be followed afterwards as a residual disease marker.

The assay is most often ordered where morphology and immunohistochemistry disagree or where the sample is small: a skin biopsy in suspected cutaneous T-cell lymphoma, a gastric biopsy in suspected MALT lymphoma, a marrow with an ambiguous infiltrate, or a lymph node with an atypical but not clearly malignant population.

links.label: van Dongen et al., Leukemia 2003: BIOMED-2 multiplex PCR for clonal immunoglobulin and T-cell receptor rearrangements
EuroClonality/BIOMED-2 guidelines for interpretation and reporting of Ig/TCR clonality testing in suspected lymphoproliferations.

records.principle: Multiplex PCR, or targeted sequencing, across the V, D and J segments of the immunoglobulin and T-cell receptor loci. A clonal population gives amplicons of one length and sequence; a polyclonal population gives a Gaussian spread of lengths. The output is a pattern, not a diagnosis.
strengths: Works on tiny and on fixed samples, including paraffin blocks and skin punch biopsies, where flow cytometry cannot be done

Combined immunoglobulin heavy-chain and kappa tubes detect virtually all clonal B-cell proliferations, even where somatic hypermutation has altered the primer binding sites, and combined T-cell receptor beta and gamma tubes detect virtually all clonal T-cell populations (van Dongen 2003)
The sequence it finds can be reused as a patient-specific residual disease marker afterwards
Standardised across European laboratories, so a result travels between centres
limitations: Clonality is not malignancy. Clonal populations occur in reactive and autoimmune conditions, in skin, in coeliac disease and in older people, and reporting a clonal result as a diagnosis is the commonest way this test does harm
A polyclonal result does not exclude lymphoma, particularly where the malignant cells are a small minority of the sample, as in classical Hodgkin lymphoma
Heavily mutated immunoglobulin genes can defeat primer binding, which is why the complementary tubes exist
It says nothing about which lymphoma it is

records.name: Immunoglobulin and T-cell receptor clonality
records.tldr: Receptor-gene patterns can provide evidence of a clonal lymphocyte population. The result must be interpreted with the tissue findings and does not diagnose cancer by itself.
records.summary:
Developing lymphocytes rearrange antigen-receptor genes. Shared rearrangements can support common ancestry, but a detected clonal pattern is not synonymous with malignancy, and a negative assay does not exclude it. Sampling, reactive expansions, multiple alleles, primer coverage and technical artifacts affect interpretation. The number of peaks is not a direct count of clones.

The European BIOMED-2 collaboration standardised the assay into 107 primers in 18 multiplex tubes covering IGH in two configurations, IGK, IGL, TCRB, TCRG and TCRD plus the BCL1-IGH and BCL2-IGH translocations, with products read by heteroduplex analysis or fragment sizing. The complementarity of the tubes is what makes the detection rate high: combined IGH and IGK tubes detect virtually all clonal B-cell proliferations even where somatic hypermutation is heavy, and combined TCRB and TCRG tubes detect virtually all clonal T-cell populations (van Dongen 2003). The EuroClonality-NGS successor sequences the amplicons rather than sizing them and produces a patient-specific sequence that can be followed afterwards as a residual disease marker.

The result is a pattern, not a diagnosis, and the commonest harm this test does is being read as one.

links.label: van Dongen et al., Leukemia 2003: BIOMED-2 multiplex PCR for clonal immunoglobulin and T-cell receptor rearrangements
EuroClonality/BIOMED-2 guidelines for interpretation and reporting of Ig/TCR clonality testing in suspected lymphoproliferations.

records.noParentReason: The readout is a pattern across the immunoglobulin and T-cell receptor loci rather than a result for one gene or protein: the question is whether the population is monoclonal, and no single parent gene answers it.

scoringRule.text: Multiplex PCR, or targeted sequencing, across the V, D and J segments, reported as clonal, polyclonal or oligoclonal, with the loci tested named. A clonal result should be read with the morphology and immunophenotype and never alone: clonal populations occur in reactive, autoimmune and age-related conditions, and a polyclonal result does not exclude a lymphoma in which the malignant cells are a small minority.
scoringRule.quote: In particular, combined application of IGH (VH-JH and DH-JH) and IGK tubes can detect virtually all clonal B-cell proliferations, even in B-cell malignancies with high levels of somatic mutations.

definedBy.label: van Dongen et al., Leukemia 2003: BIOMED-2 multiplex PCR for clonal immunoglobulin and T-cell receptor rearrangements

records.forPatient: A clonal result is a piece of evidence, not a verdict. It is most useful when a biopsy is small or the appearance is borderline, and it is read together with everything else. A report that says clonal does not by itself mean cancer.

records.name: DNA methylation arrays and beta values (450k, EPIC)
records.tldr: Methylation arrays compare modified and unmodified probe signals at selected DNA sites. Their beta values are assay signal ratios, not direct counts of cancer cells.
records.summary: The Illumina Infinium methylation assay uses BeadChip technology for genome-wide profiling of human DNA methylation, quantifying methylation at many loci (Wikipedia); the 450k array covers about 450,000 CpG sites and the EPIC array about 850,000. Each site's beta value is the methylated signal over total signal. DNA methylation in promoters typically represses transcription and is a stable record of cell identity, which is why methylation classifiers work for brain tumours and why methylation adds tissue-of-origin information to expression.

links.label: A genomic sequencing protocol that yields a positive display of 5-methylcytosine residues in individual DNA strands.

notes: A beta value is a processed methylated-signal versus total-signal measure; background handling and assay chemistry matter. Standard bisulfite does not distinguish 5-methylcytosine from 5-hydroxymethylcytosine. Mixed-cell proportions, genomic context and platform coverage limit interpretation; a value is not a cancer-cell silencing percentage.
